---
title: "2.4 · Self-consistent Maxwell-equation solution"
subtitle: "A self-consistent Maxwell-equation approach"
---
We derive the complex refractive index of a dielectric using two ingredients: Maxwell's equations and the Lorentz electron-oscillator model. The logic is
$$
\text{Maxwell wave equation}
\longrightarrow
\text{Lorentz oscillator}
\longrightarrow \widetilde{\mathbf P}(\omega)
\longrightarrow \chi(\omega)
\longrightarrow n(\omega).
$$
Throughout this page, ordinary time-dependent symbols denote physical, real quantities. A tilde denotes a time-independent complex amplitude at frequency $\omega$. Because the light is polarized along $z$, we write
$$
\mathbf E(x,t)=\operatorname{Re}\!\left[\widetilde E(x)e^{-i\omega t}\right]\hat{\mathbf z},
\qquad
\widetilde{\mathbf E}(x)=\widetilde E(x)\hat{\mathbf z}.
$$ {#eq-maxwell-complex-convention}
Thus $\widetilde E$ is the scalar $z$-component of the complex field amplitude, whereas $\widetilde{\mathbf E}$ is the corresponding vector. We use the same convention for the dipole moment and polarization.

## General wave equation in a medium

### Maxwell equations
In a material medium, Maxwell's equations are
$$
\boldsymbol{\nabla}\cdot\mathbf D=\rho_f,
$$ {#eq-gauss-electric}
$$
\boldsymbol{\nabla}\cdot\mathbf B=0,
$$ {#eq-gauss-magnetic}
$$
\boldsymbol{\nabla}\times\mathbf E
=-\frac{\partial\mathbf B}{\partial t},
$$ {#eq-faraday}
$$
\boldsymbol{\nabla}\times\mathbf H
=\mathbf J_f+\frac{\partial\mathbf D}{\partial t}.
$$ {#eq-ampere-maxwell}
The electric displacement is
$$
\mathbf D=\epsilon_0\mathbf E+\mathbf P,
$$ {#eq-displacement}
where $\mathbf P$ is the polarization of the medium. For a nonmagnetic medium,
$$
\mathbf B=\mu_0\mathbf H.
$$ {#eq-nonmagnetic-medium}

### Wave equation with polarization

Consider a region with no free charge and no free current,
$$
\rho_f=0,
\qquad
\mathbf J_f=0.
$$ {#eq-no-free-sources}
Take the curl of Faraday's law, @eq-faraday:
$$
\boldsymbol{\nabla}\times
\left(\boldsymbol{\nabla}\times\mathbf E\right)
=-\frac{\partial}{\partial t}
\left(\boldsymbol{\nabla}\times\mathbf B\right).
$$ {#eq-curl-faraday}
Using @eq-nonmagnetic-medium and the Ampere-Maxwell law, @eq-ampere-maxwell,
$$
\boldsymbol{\nabla}\times
\left(\boldsymbol{\nabla}\times\mathbf E\right)
=-\mu_0\frac{\partial^2\mathbf D}{\partial t^2}.
$$ {#eq-curl-wave-step}
Use the vector identity
$$
\boldsymbol{\nabla}\times
\left(\boldsymbol{\nabla}\times\mathbf E\right)
=
\boldsymbol{\nabla}
\left(\boldsymbol{\nabla}\cdot\mathbf E\right)
-\nabla^2\mathbf E.
$$ {#eq-vector-identity}
For a homogeneous dielectric with no free charge, $\boldsymbol{\nabla}\cdot\mathbf D=0$. If the dielectric response is spatially uniform, this gives $\boldsymbol{\nabla}\cdot\mathbf E=0$. Therefore @eq-curl-wave-step becomes
$$
\nabla^2\mathbf E
-\mu_0\frac{\partial^2\mathbf D}{\partial t^2}=0.
$$ {#eq-wave-D}
Substituting @eq-displacement gives
$$
\boxed{
\nabla^2\mathbf E
-\frac{1}{c^2}\frac{\partial^2\mathbf E}{\partial t^2}
=\mu_0\frac{\partial^2\mathbf P}{\partial t^2}
},
$$ {#eq-wave-polarization}
where
$$
c^2=\frac{1}{\mu_0\epsilon_0}.
$$ {#eq-speed-light}
@eq-wave-polarization is the general wave equation we will use for a homogeneous, nonmagnetic dielectric with no free charges or currents. At this point we have not yet assumed any specific relation between $\mathbf P$ and $\mathbf E$. We now obtain that relation from the Lorentz oscillator model.

#### $\nabla^2\mathbf E$ for a plane wave
{{< include vector-calculus.qmd >}}

## Lorentz electron-oscillator model

Consider a bound electron of charge $-e$, mass $m$, natural frequency $\omega_0$, and damping constant $\gamma$. Its electric dipole moment along the polarization direction is $p=-ez$, where $z$ is the electron's displacement from equilibrium. The equation of motion for the dipole moment is
$$
\ddot{p}+2\gamma\dot{p}+\omega_0^2p=\frac{e^2}{m}E(t).
$$ {#eq-lorentz-oscillator}
A crucial point is the meaning of the driving field $E(t)$ in @eq-lorentz-oscillator. In the present Maxwell-equation treatment, we seek a **self-consistent field inside the medium**. Therefore, neglecting microscopic local-field corrections, $E(t)$ is the **total macroscopic electric field in the material**: the field that remains after the incident field and the fields produced by all of the polarized atoms have combined. It is not assumed in advance to be the unperturbed vacuum incident field.

It is useful to compare this with the [thin-sheet derivation](optical-dispersion.qmd). In that approximation, the oscillators in **every sheet** are driven  by the **unperturbed vacuum field** plus the total induced field radiated by the sheets on its left side, neglecting radiations from the sheet on its right side.

The Maxwell-equation treatment is different. Here $E(t)$ in @eq-lorentz-oscillator is the **self-consistent macroscopic field inside the medium**, and the polarization generated by the medium is part of the same field that drives the oscillators. 

## From polarization to the complex refractive index
For harmonic time dependence $e^{-i\omega t}$, @eq-lorentz-oscillator gives the dipole response
$$
\widetilde{\mathbf p}(x)=\alpha(\omega)\widetilde{\mathbf E}(x),
\qquad
\alpha(\omega)=\frac{e^2}{m(\omega_0^2-\omega^2-2i\gamma\omega)}.
$$ {#eq-polarization-response}
Here $\widetilde{\mathbf p}(x)=\widetilde p(x)\hat{\mathbf z}$. For $N$ oscillators per unit volume, the polarization is
$$
\widetilde{\mathbf P}(x)=N\widetilde{\mathbf p}(x)
=\epsilon_0\chi(\omega)\widetilde{\mathbf E}(x).
$$ {#eq-linear-polarization-vector}
Define the vacuum wave number as
$$
k_0=\frac{\omega}{c}.
$$ {#eq-vacuum-wave-number}
Substituting the polarization relation into @eq-wave-polarization gives
$$
\nabla^2\widetilde{\mathbf E}
+k_0^2
\left[1+\chi(\omega)\right]\widetilde{\mathbf E}=0.
$$ {#eq-frequency-wave}
For a plane wave propagating along $+x$ with its electric field polarized along $z$, choose the phase origin so that $E_0$ is real and positive. Its complex spatial amplitude is
$$
\widetilde{\mathbf E}(x)
=E_0e^{ikx}\hat{\mathbf z},
$$ {#eq-plane-wave}
substitution into @eq-frequency-wave gives
$$
k^2
=k_0^2
\left[1+\chi(\omega)\right].
$$ {#eq-dispersion-k}

Define the refractive index by
$$
k=nk_0.
$$ {#eq-index-definition}
Then
$$
\boxed{n^2(\omega)=1+\chi(\omega)}.
$$ {#eq-index-susceptibility}

Because $\chi(\omega)$ is complex, the refractive index is also complex. Write
$$
n=n'+in'',
$$ {#eq-complex-index}
where
$$
n'=\mathrm{Re}\left[\sqrt{1+\chi}\right],\qquad n''=\mathrm{Im}\left[\sqrt{1+\chi}\right].
$$

## Propagation and absorption

Using @eq-index-definition and @eq-complex-index, the complex wave number is
$$
k=k_0(n'+in'').
$$ {#eq-complex-wave-number}

Therefore the complex plane wave @eq-plane-wave becomes
$$
\widetilde E(x)
=E_0
\exp\left(-k_0n''x\right)
\exp\left(ik_0n'x\right).
$$ {#eq-complex-propagating-field}
Taking the real part gives the physical electric field,
$$
\boxed{
E(x,t)
=E_0
\exp\left(-k_0n''x\right)
\cos\left(k_0n'x-\omega t\right)
}.
$$ {#eq-physical-field}
Thus $n'$ determines the phase velocity and dispersion, while $n''$ determines attenuation and absorption.

Since the cycle-averaged intensity is proportional to $|\widetilde E|^2$, @eq-complex-propagating-field gives
$$
I(x)=I_0
\exp\left(-2k_0n''x\right).
$$ {#eq-intensity-decay}
For a medium containing $N$ absorbers per unit volume, define the absorption cross section $\sigma_{\mathrm{abs}}$ through the Beer--Lambert law
$$
I(x)=I_0e^{-N\sigma_{\mathrm{abs}}x}.
$$ {#eq-beer-cross-section}
Comparing @eq-intensity-decay and @eq-beer-cross-section gives
$$
\boxed{
\sigma_{\mathrm{abs}}
=\frac{2k_0n''}{N}
}.
$$ {#eq-absorption-cross-section-index}

## Dilute-medium approximation

If
$$
|\chi|\ll1,
$$ {#eq-small-susceptibility}
then from @eq-index-susceptibility,
$$
n=\sqrt{1+\chi}
\simeq1+\frac{\chi}{2}.
$$ {#eq-index-expansion}
Therefore,
$$
\boxed{
n'\simeq1+\frac{\chi'}{2}
},
$$ {#eq-index-real-approx}
and
$$
\boxed{
n''\simeq\frac{\chi''}{2}
}.
$$ {#eq-index-imag-approx}
This is what we obtained from the thin sheets approximation.

## Summary

The general Maxwell wave equation in a dielectric is @eq-wave-polarization,
$$
\nabla^2\mathbf E
-\frac{1}{c^2}\frac{\partial^2\mathbf E}{\partial t^2}
=\mu_0\frac{\partial^2\mathbf P}{\partial t^2}.
$$
The Lorentz oscillator @eq-lorentz-oscillator then gives the polarization response @eq-polarization-response. This naturally defines the complex susceptibility through @eq-linear-polarization-vector,
$$
\widetilde{\mathbf P}(x)
=\epsilon_0\chi(\omega)\widetilde{\mathbf E}(x).
$$ 
where
$$
\begin{aligned}
\chi(\omega)
=&\frac{Ne^2}{\epsilon_0 m(\omega_0^2-\omega^2-2i\gamma\omega)}\\
\simeq&-\frac{Ne^2}{2\epsilon_0m\omega_0}\frac{1}{\Delta+i\gamma}.
\end{aligned}
$$
Substituting this constitutive relation back into the Maxwell wave equation gives
$$
\boxed{n^2(\omega)=1+\chi(\omega)}.
$$
The damping term produces a phase lag between the electron motion and the driving electric field. This makes $\chi$ complex. Through Maxwell's wave equation, the refractive index also becomes complex: its real part describes phase propagation and dispersion, while its imaginary part describes absorption.
